metadata.title: Gaining tolerance of immigrants through simulating migratory experiences: Quasi-experimental evidence from secondary school classrooms

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a classroom-based quasi-experimental design with 5 teachers and 148 matched students in Sweden, collected via self-selection rather than a probability sample. The manuscript does not report the use of any complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and it does not describe a stratified/clustered weighting scheme for population-representative inference. Because the analysis is based on a small, convenience classroom sample and the statistical models are standard regression/Wilcoxon tests rather than ILSA scaling, analysts should not treat the results as nationally representative. For any re-analysis using ICCS 2022 microdata, appropriate student weights and replicate weights would be required, but this paper’s intervention dataset is not an ICCS microdata extract.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are Likert-type attitude scales (ATI, political tolerance, social tolerance) and their pre/post scores, not cognitive achievement scores generated with Plausible Values in ICCS/PISA-style scaling. The paper reports missing counts in descriptive tables (e.g., Table 2) but does not explicitly state the missing-data handling rule used for the inferential models (e.g., complete-case vs imputation). This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data treatment in the regression and moderation analyses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were recruited through school-research collaborative networks in spring 2024 (self-selection of schools). Of 225 students who completed the pretest, intervention, and posttest, the dataset was reduced to 148 after controlling for participant matching across pre- and posttests; attrition was mainly due to incorrect/missing anonymised ID codes and some missing parental consent for students under 15. The intervention was delivered in students’ regular classrooms by 5 teachers during a fall 2024 six-week window, with pretest immediately before and posttest immediately after the simulation module. The analytic sample is the matched subset used for the quantitative analyses reported in Tables 2–3 and Appendix A.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2022-derived attitude measures (Sweden; secondary/upper-secondary students aged 14–19; pretest-posttest)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical regression (Jamovi): Model fit R2=0.737 (Model D), overall model F(24,110)=12.9, p<0.001. Interaction term: B=0.303, p=0.025, standardized beta β=0.125. Wilcoxon signed-rank (pre vs post): Mdn post=39 vs pre=38, W=4562, p=0.005, rank-biserial r=0.2995.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2022-derived attitude measures in a Swedish secondary-school pretest–posttest design, the study leveraged baseline ATI, perceived learning, parents’ political interest, and simulation exposure (playing time) plus a moderation interaction between prior knowledge and playing time to explain ATI posttest levels, finding that ATI increased significantly after the simulation (W=4562, p=0.005, r=0.2995) and that perceived learning and playing time were significant predictors in the final regression model (interaction B=0.303, p=0.025). This indicates that well-briefed, sufficiently sustained simulation-based migratory experiences can improve students’ tolerance toward immigrants, though the study’s quasi-experimental design and missing-data reporting limit causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: ICCS 2022-derived attitude measures (Sweden; secondary/upper-secondary students aged 14–19; pretest-posttest)
main_findings.target_variable: Social tolerance towards immigrants posttest score
main_findings.performance_metrics: Wilcoxon signed-rank (pre vs post): Mdn post=28 vs pre=27, W=4432, p=0.002, rank-biserial r=0.3288. Political tolerance Wilcoxon: p=0.927 (non-significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2022-derived attitude measures in a Swedish secondary-school pretest–posttest design, the study leveraged the intervention’s simulated migratory exposure and related learning mechanisms to assess social tolerance, finding that social tolerance increased significantly after the simulation (W=4432, p=0.002, r=0.3288) while political tolerance showed no significant change (p=0.927). This indicates that simulation-based indirect contact may be more effective for interpersonal/social dimensions of tolerance than for political-rights attitudes, suggesting educators should target social-empathy and perspective-taking components when designing migration-related lessons.

data.outcome_summary: This study evaluates a quasi-experimental, classroom-based intervention in Sweden using ICCS 2022-derived attitude scales for secondary/upper-secondary students (ages 14–19). Five teachers implemented a 60-minute browser-based simulation (“Real Lives”) in fall 2024, with pretest immediately before and posttest immediately after; the analytic matched sample comprised 148 students. Outcomes were attitudes towards immigrants (ATI; composite of political and social tolerance) and social tolerance separately, analyzed with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and hierarchical regression (Jamovi). ATI increased significantly from pre to post (Mdn 38→39; W=4562, p=0.005, r=0.2995), and social tolerance also increased (Mdn 27→28; W=4432, p=0.002, r=0.3288), whereas political tolerance did not (p=0.927). In the final regression model, perceived learning and playing time (plus a prior-knowledge moderation interaction) were significant predictors of ATI posttest levels (interaction B=0.303, p=0.025). Limitations include no control group/randomization, convenience sampling, and missing-data handling not explicitly reported for inferential models.
